blocks.text: A nebulizer is a device that converts liquid medication into an aerosol that a patient can inhale into the respiratory tract.
It is commonly used to deliver bronchodilators and selected other inhaled medications in patients with respiratory conditions such as asthma and COPD.
Typical OSCE instruction: “Identify the instrument, explain its principle, demonstrate its assembly and use, list the medications administered through it, and discuss precautions and complications.”
A. Jet nebulizer
Uses compressed gas, usually air or oxygen, to convert liquid medication into aerosol.
Uses: Commonly used in emergency departments, wards and home treatment for selected respiratory conditions.
B. Ultrasonic nebulizer
Uses high-frequency vibrations to generate aerosol.
Limitation: Not suitable for every medication or suspension; compatibility depends on the device and formulation.
C. Vibrating mesh nebulizer
Pushes liquid through a fine vibrating mesh to produce aerosol.
Advantages: Often portable, quiet and efficient, but the mesh requires appropriate cleaning and maintenance.

rows: Produces the energy needed to generate aerosol.
Connects the compressor to the nebulizer chamber in jet systems.
Allows aerosol delivery when a mouthpiece is unsuitable.
Provides the driving gas in jet systems.
Helps prevent dust or contaminants entering the compressor.

blocks.text: OSCE distinction: The nebulizer produces the aerosol; the mask or mouthpiece delivers it to the patient.
The device transforms a liquid formulation into small aerosol droplets that can be inhaled.

blocks.title: The amount of medication reaching the lungs depends on factors such as:

items.text: The medication and formulation.
The nebulizer design and output.
Patient breathing pattern and cooperation.
Mask fit or mouthpiece seal.
Treatment duration and residual medication volume.

blocks.text: Nebulizers do not automatically deliver the entire nominal medication dose to the lungs.

items.text: Administration of inhaled bronchodilators during selected asthma exacerbations.
Delivery of inhaled medication in selected COPD exacerbations.
Treatment of bronchospasm when a nebulizer is clinically appropriate.
Delivery of certain inhaled medications to patients unable to use other delivery systems effectively.
Administration of selected specialist inhaled treatments when the medication and device are compatible.

blocks.title: Examples of medications that may be nebulized include:

items.text: Salbutamol (albuterol): Short-acting beta₂ agonist bronchodilator.
Ipratropium bromide: Short-acting muscarinic antagonist bronchodilator.
Budesonide: Inhaled corticosteroid in suitable formulations and clinical circumstances.
Hypertonic saline: Used in selected conditions under appropriate protocols.

blocks.text: Medication selection depends on the diagnosis, patient age, severity, prescribed regimen and local guidelines.
Important: Not every liquid medication can be nebulized. Use only formulations intended or specifically approved for the device and route.

items.text: Delivers medication directly to the respiratory tract.
Can be used by patients who struggle to coordinate inhalation with an inhaler.
Can be administered through an appropriate mask to young children.
Allows tidal breathing during treatment.
Can deliver certain medication doses that are appropriate for nebulization.
Useful in selected acute-care and specialist respiratory settings.
Treatment generally takes longer than using a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer.
Equipment requires cleaning, maintenance and appropriate storage.
Incorrect assembly can reduce medication delivery.
Aerosol can escape into the surrounding environment, exposing carers or staff to medication.
Some devices are noisy or require a power source.
Poor mask fit and crying can reduce effective drug delivery in children.
Contaminated equipment can transmit infection.
Nebulization may increase heart rate or cause tremor when beta₂ agonists are used.

blocks.text: High-yield comparison: For many patients with asthma, a correctly used metered-dose inhaler with a spacer is at least as effective as a nebulizer for delivering short-acting bronchodilators in mild-to-moderate exacerbations. A nebulizer is not automatically the superior option.

subsections.subsection_title: 8. How to assemble and use a nebulizer

blocks.text: 0 of 15 steps completed
1. Perform hand hygiene, introduce yourself, confirm patient identity, explain the procedure and obtain consent.
2. Assess the patient’s respiratory status, including respiratory rate, work of breathing, pulse and oxygen saturation when indicated.
3. Check the prescription, medication name, dose, expiry date, formulation and allergies.
4. Inspect the nebulizer, chamber, tubing, mask or mouthpiece and power or gas supply.
5. Perform hand hygiene and use appropriate protective equipment.
6. Assemble the device according to the manufacturer's instructions.
7. Place the prescribed medication into the chamber using aseptic technique and add compatible diluent only if indicated.
8. Connect the chamber to the compressor or appropriate gas supply.
9. Position the patient upright if tolerated and fit the mask securely or place the mouthpiece between the lips.
10. Start the device and confirm that aerosol is being generated.
11. Encourage calm, regular breathing through the mouthpiece or well-fitted mask.
12. Monitor symptoms, respiratory effort, pulse and oxygen saturation as clinically appropriate.
13. Continue until the device's specified treatment endpoint is reached; avoid relying solely on the appearance of visible mist.
14. Turn off the device, remove the interface and reassess the patient's response.
15. Dispose of single-use components appropriately and clean, disinfect or store reusable parts according to manufacturer instructions.
**Important practical points**

items.text: Never put an unprescribed medication or an unsuitable liquid into the chamber.
Use sterile fluid where required by the medication, device instructions and clinical protocol.
Do not mix medications unless compatibility has been established and the prescription or protocol permits it.
Do not allow the chamber to tip over and spill its contents.
A mouthpiece may provide more effective delivery than a poorly fitting mask when the patient can use it.
A child should be calm and the mask should fit closely. Holding a mask near the face without a proper seal can substantially reduce drug delivery.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Nebulizer versus metered-dose inhaler with spacer

blocks.text: Useful when prolonged tidal breathing or a particular nebulized formulation is appropriate, or when a patient cannot effectively use another delivery system.
Often faster, portable and effective for bronchodilator delivery in asthma. A spacer reduces the coordination required between actuation and inhalation.

Neither device is appropriate for every patient or medication. In severe respiratory distress, the choice of delivery system should follow the emergency protocol and the patient's ability to use it effectively.

There are no universal absolute contraindications to nebulizer equipment itself. The main considerations are medication-specific contraindications, device compatibility and the patient's clinical condition.

items.text: Confirm the correct medication and dose.
Check for allergies and relevant contraindications to the prescribed drug.
Use caution with beta₂ agonists in patients with significant tachyarrhythmias or other relevant cardiovascular problems.
Ensure appropriate oxygen monitoring when clinically indicated.
If oxygen is used as the driving gas, consider the patient's risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure and follow the prescribed oxygen target.
In patients with suspected or known infectious respiratory disease, follow appropriate ventilation, PPE and aerosol-generating procedure policies.

items.text: Use an age-appropriate mask or mouthpiece.
Ensure a good mask seal without obstructing the nose or mouth.
Keep the child as calm and upright as tolerated.
Monitor respiratory effort, oxygen saturation and heart rate when indicated.

Use weight- or age-appropriate prescribed doses according to the applicable guideline.

In neonates, use only a device and medication appropriate to the neonatal indication and specialist protocol.

blocks.text: Emergency pediatric point: A child with severe asthma who becomes exhausted, confused, cyanosed or develops markedly reduced air entry needs immediate emergency management. Nebulization alone is not sufficient treatment for life-threatening asthma.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. Common OSCE questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is a nebulizer?
A device that converts liquid medication into an aerosol for inhalation into the respiratory tract.
Q2. Name three types of nebulizers.
Jet, ultrasonic and vibrating mesh nebulizers.
Q3. Name two common bronchodilators administered by nebulizer.
Salbutamol and ipratropium bromide.
Q4. Why might a spacer be preferred to a nebulizer in asthma?
A metered-dose inhaler with a spacer is often faster, portable and effective when used correctly, including in many children.
Q5. What are the adverse effects of repeated high-dose salbutamol?
Tachycardia, tremor and hypokalaemia; other metabolic effects may occur in severe exacerbations.
Q6. Why must a nebulizer be cleaned properly?
To prevent contamination, cross-infection and obstruction or malfunction of the device.
Q7. What should you do if a child deteriorates during nebulization?

Assess airway, breathing and circulation immediately, call for appropriate emergency assistance, and institute urgent management. Do not continue routine administration without reassessing the cause of deterioration.

subsections.subsection_title: 14. Common mistakes that lose OSCE marks

items.text: Failing to check the prescription, drug, dose or expiry date.
Incorrectly assembling the chamber or tubing.
Using an unsuitable solution or mixing incompatible medications.
Failing to secure the mask.
Neglecting to monitor the patient during treatment.
Failing to reassess after administration.
Ignoring tachycardia or worsening respiratory distress.
Sharing or storing contaminated equipment.
Assuming that a nebulizer is always better than an inhaler with a spacer.
